name: TypeScript
title: TypeScript (6.0)

type.text: **Structural typing decouples from concrete types**: Can pass any object with right shape
**Union types separate cases**: `string | number` makes alternatives explicit, and a discriminated union is a checked sum type
**Generics enable parametric polymorphism**: Decouple from concrete types
**`strictNullChecks` makes absence a checked case**: `string` and `string | null` are different types, so a possibly-absent value must be narrowed before use, and `T10` is absent
**`any` is an explicit opt-out**: `strict` bans an implicit `any`, but a written `any` still drops the check at that spot
**Type assertions couple to implementation**: `as Type` forces coupling
**The artifact carries no types**: Types are erased at run time, so a consumer recovers a type by convention (`T7`)
**A method call dispatches on the run-time value**: An interface declares the method, but the call reaches the prototype's implementation at run time (`T3`)
Inherits the engine rule: string length and indexing count UTF-16 units

construction.text: **Object literals decouple construction**: `{ name: "Alice", age: 30 }` without classes
**Class constructors can have side effects**: Nothing prevents coupled initialization
**Dependency injection requires manual wiring**: No built-in mechanism
**Module side effects**: Imports can execute code, coupling load order
**Objects are mutable unless marked `readonly` (C2)**: `readonly` is opt-in, so any holder of a reference can change the object
**One value, many names**: objects and arrays move by reference under the type annotations, which name the type, not the sharing

memory.text: **JavaScript GC decouples memory**: Generational GC (V8, SpiderMonkey, etc.)
**No manual memory management**: Can't have use-after-free
**Closure captures extend lifetimes**: Closures hold references, prevent collection
**Event listeners create memory leaks**: Forgotten listeners couple to DOM/event system
**Circular references with DOM**: Can create leaks if not careful with event handlers

**Collection follows the JavaScript runtime's schedule (M2)**: A value stays allocated until V8's collector decides, and the pause is non-deterministic, so the heap's release schedule is not the program's to name
**`using` ties a release to the scope (M3 absent)**: TypeScript 5.2 adds `using` and `await using`, so a value with a `Symbol.dispose` method releases at block exit

error.text: **Exceptions are unchecked**: No `throws` clause, errors hidden from type system
**Result types exist but not idiomatic**: Libraries like `neverthrow` exist but uncommon
**Promise rejection is unchecked**: Async errors not tracked by types

concurrency.text: **Async/await separates sync from async**: `async function` makes concurrency explicit
**Promises don't track errors**: `Promise<T>` doesn't show failure type
**The event loop is the only unit of work (K1)**: Single-threaded, so a long callback blocks every other task and no second core is available for CPU-bound work, and callbacks create order coupling
**Shared module state has no concurrency discipline (K2, K3)**: A module-level binding is reachable from every callback, and nothing detects a race across interleaved tasks

platform.text: **The compiler is open source and emits a standard target**: `tsc` is developed in the open under Apache 2.0, and its output is ECMAScript, so no proprietary runtime is required
**The emitted code runs on every major engine**: The output runs on V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore and on Node.js, Deno, and Bun alike
**Several tools compile TypeScript**: `tsc`, `esbuild`, `swc`, and Node.js type stripping all accept `.ts` source, so the build step is not locked to one implementation
**No language runtime is deployed**: Type checking happens at build time and the artifact is JavaScript, so nothing of TypeScript ships to the platform
**The compiler runs on all three desktop platforms**: One npm package covers Windows, macOS, and Linux

performance.text: **JavaScript runtime**: Inherits JS performance characteristics, JIT optimization
**Type erasure**: No runtime cost but also no runtime enforcement
**Unpredictable GC**: No control over pause times
**Bundle size couples to libraries**: Frontend deployment couples to dependency graph

ecosystem.text: **Build tools mature**: Webpack, Vite, esbuild, tsc
**Too many build tools**: Choice couples to toolchain complexity
A node-gyp addon in the dependency tree binds to a Node major, and the crossing-major path is Node-API [@nodeAbiStability; @nodeNapi]

evolution.text: **Lib versioning**: `@types` packages couple to library versions

domain.text: **Excellent for frontend**: Industry standard for React, Angular, Vue

learning.text: **Type system complexity**: Conditional types, mapped types can be confusing
**Familiar to C#/Java devs**: Similar type system concepts

syntax.text: **Type annotations can be verbose**: Generics get noisy
**Type inference**: Often don't need explicit types
**Any escape hatch**: Too easy to bypass types

testing.text: **Runtime vs compile-time gap**: Types don't catch runtime issues

security.text: **Prototype pollution**: Object mutation can create vulnerabilities
**Dependency vulnerabilities**: Npm ecosystem size couples to attack surface
Inherits the JavaScript engine rule: double arithmetic, silent integer change above 2^53

tradeoffs: **Type Safety vs. Runtime Reality**: Types are documentation only, no runtime enforcement couples safety to discipline
**Gradual Typing vs. Type Holes**: `any` escape hatch couples strict code to untyped code
**JavaScript Compatibility vs. Type Safety**: Must support all JS patterns, even unsafe ones
**Type System Complexity vs. JavaScript Simplicity**: Advanced types (conditional, mapped) couple to TS-specific knowledge
**Build Step vs. Simplicity**: Compilation adds complexity, couples deployment to build tools
verdict: TypeScript keeps less of JavaScript's type coupling than JavaScript does: `strict` makes absence a checked case, structural typing and discriminated unions remove the dynamic-typing and sum-type mechanisms, and `using` ties a release to the scope. What its type layer cannot remove is the JavaScript runtime's: a single-threaded event loop, a collector the program cannot schedule, unowned mutable objects, and failures that no type tracks. TypeScript therefore carries the same Core Coupling score as JavaScript — 28 — and both stay in the lowest band, because the runtime coupling dominates.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The compiler emits JavaScript source the engine parses
A node-gyp addon in the dependency tree binds to one Node major version
Node-API is ABI stable across Node major versions
